prompt: What is a nonpolar covalent bond?

choices.text: A covalent bond in which the electron pair is shared equally by the two atoms
A covalent bond in which the electron pair stays nearer one atom than the other
choices.why: That unequal sharing describes a polar covalent bond. In a nonpolar bond the electrons are balanced between the two nuclei.

choices.text: A bond in which one atom transfers an electron completely to the other
choices.why: Transferring an electron makes ions and an ionic bond. In a covalent bond the electrons are shared.

choices.text: A covalent bond in which neither atom has any lone pairs of electrons
choices.why: Polarity is about how evenly the bonding pair is shared, not about lone pairs. F2 has three lone pairs on each F atom, yet its bond is nonpolar.

explanation: The equal sharing of electrons in a covalent bond is called a nonpolar covalent bond. In H2, for example, the two identical nuclei attract the bonding pair by the same amount.

prompt: In the HF molecule, the F atom attracts the shared pair of electrons much more strongly than the H atom does, so the electrons stay nearer the F atom. Which description of the bond in HF is correct?

choices.text: Polar covalent, with a partial negative charge (δ−) on F and a partial positive charge (δ+) on H
Polar covalent, with a partial positive charge (δ+) on F and a partial negative charge (δ−) on H
choices.why: The electrons are nearer the F atom, so the F end takes on the partial negative charge, not the partial positive one.

choices.text: Nonpolar covalent, because the two atoms share a single pair of electrons between them
choices.why: Sharing one pair makes it a single bond, but the pair is not shared equally. Unequal sharing makes a bond polar.

choices.text: Ionic, with a full positive charge on the H atom and a full negative charge on the F atom
choices.why: The electrons are still shared, only unequally. That gives partial charges, δ+ and δ−, rather than the full charges of ions.

explanation: Because the shared electrons sit nearer F, the F side of the molecule takes on a partial negative charge (δ−) and the H side a partial positive charge (δ+). Unequal sharing like this is a polar covalent bond.

prompt: How is a partial charge, written δ+ or δ−, different from the charge on an ion such as Na+ or Cl−?

choices.text: It is less than a full charge, and it comes from shared electrons sitting nearer one atom, not from an electron being transferred.
It is a full 1+ or 1− charge, written with δ to show that the atom is part of a molecule.
choices.why: δ marks only part of a charge. A full 1+ or 1− charge comes from an electron actually moving from one atom to another.

choices.text: It comes from an atom gaining or losing part of a proton when the covalent bond forms.
choices.why: Protons don't move when bonds form. Partial charges come from where the shared electrons spend their time.

choices.text: It appears only in bonds between two atoms of the same element, such as the bond in Cl2.
choices.why: Two identical atoms attract the shared electrons equally, so their bond has no partial charges. Partial charges appear when different atoms share electrons unequally.

explanation: In a polar covalent bond the shared electrons are nearer one atom, so that end takes on a partial negative charge (δ−) and the other end a partial positive charge (δ+). An ion's full charge comes from an electron actually transferring from one atom to another.

prompt: Ammonia, NH3, has three N–H bonds. The electronegativity of N is 3.04 and that of H is 2.2. Which atom carries the partial negative charge (δ−) in each N–H bond?

choices.text: N, because it has the higher electronegativity
H, because it has the lower electronegativity
choices.why: A lower electronegativity means a weaker pull on the shared electrons, so the electrons are drawn away from H and it becomes δ+.

choices.text: H, because the shared electrons stay nearer the smaller atom
choices.why: The electrons stay nearer the atom that attracts them more strongly, which is the one with the higher electronegativity, N.

choices.text: Neither, because the N–H bond is nonpolar
choices.why: N and H have different electronegativities (difference 3.04 − 2.2 = 0.84), so the electrons are not shared equally and the bond is polar.

explanation: The atom with the higher electronegativity attracts the shared electrons more strongly. N (3.04) pulls the electrons toward itself, so N is δ− and each H is δ+.

prompt: Chlorine is bonded to hydrogen in HCl and to oxygen in Cl2O, whose structure is Cl–O–Cl. The electronegativities are H 2.2, Cl 3.16, and O 3.44. What partial charge does a Cl atom carry in each molecule?

choices.text: δ− in HCl and δ+ in Cl2O
δ− in both molecules
choices.why: Whether Cl is δ− depends on its partner. O (3.44) is more electronegative than Cl (3.16), so in Cl2O the electrons are pulled toward O and the Cl atoms are δ+.

choices.text: δ+ in HCl and δ− in Cl2O
choices.why: This reverses the rule. The more electronegative atom of a bond is δ−: Cl rather than H in HCl, and O rather than Cl in Cl2O.

choices.text: δ+ in both molecules
choices.why: Cl (3.16) is more electronegative than H (2.2), so in HCl the shared electrons are pulled toward Cl, making it δ−.

explanation: The more electronegative atom in a bond is δ−. In HCl, Cl (3.16) outpulls H (2.2), so Cl is δ−; in Cl2O, O (3.44) outpulls Cl (3.16), so the Cl atoms are δ+.

prompt: What does an element's electronegativity tell you?

choices.text: How strongly its atoms attract electrons; a higher number means a stronger attraction
How strongly its atoms attract electrons; a lower number means a stronger attraction
choices.why: The scale runs the other way: the higher the electronegativity, the more strongly an atom attracts electrons.

choices.text: How much energy is needed to break a covalent bond to one of its atoms
choices.why: That is bond energy. Electronegativity measures attraction for electrons, and it is a unitless number, not an energy.

choices.text: How many electrons its atoms share when they form covalent bonds
choices.why: The number of electrons shared depends on how many bonds an atom forms. Electronegativity measures how strongly the atom attracts electrons.

explanation: Electronegativity is a scale for judging how strongly atoms of an element attract electrons. It is a unitless number; the higher the number, the more an atom attracts electrons.

prompt: Where on the periodic table are the most electronegative elements found?

choices.text: In the upper right
In the lower left
choices.why: The lower left holds the least electronegative elements, such as Cs (0.79).

choices.text: In the upper left
choices.why: Elements at the far left attract electrons weakly: Li is only 0.98, while F at the upper right is 3.98.

choices.text: In the lower right
choices.why: Electronegativity is greater near the top of a group: I (2.66) is less electronegative than F (3.98) at the top of the same group.

explanation: The more electronegative elements are in the upper right of the periodic table, such as F (3.98) and O (3.44), while the less electronegative elements are in the lower left, such as Cs (0.79).

prompt: What happens to a bond as the electronegativity difference between its two atoms gets larger?

choices.text: The electrons are pulled more toward one atom, and at a large enough difference an electron transfers, making the bond ionic.
The electrons are divided more equally between the two atoms, so the bond becomes less polar.
choices.why: A larger difference means one atom pulls much harder than the other, so the sharing becomes less equal and the bond more polar.

choices.text: The two atoms share more pairs of electrons, so a single bond turns into a double or triple bond.
choices.why: Electronegativity difference affects how evenly a bond's electrons are shared, not how many pairs are shared.

choices.text: The more electronegative atom becomes δ+, since it holds the shared electrons less tightly.
choices.why: The more electronegative atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly, so it is the δ− end of the bond.

explanation: The electronegativity difference judges the degree of polarity. The greater the difference, the more unequally the electrons are shared; a bond may be so polar that an electron actually transfers from one atom to the other, forming an ionic bond.

prompt: Sand and quartz are made of silicon and oxygen atoms joined by Si–O bonds. The electronegativity of Si is 1.9 and that of O is 3.44. How would the Si–O bond be classified?

choices.text: Definitely polar covalent
Slightly polar covalent
choices.why: Slightly polar bonds have differences of 0.4 or less. Here the difference is 3.44 − 1.9 = 1.54.

choices.text: Likely ionic
choices.why: A bond is likely ionic only when the difference is greater than 1.9. Don't compare Si's own value, 1.9, with the boundary; the difference is 1.54.

choices.text: Nonpolar covalent
choices.why: Si and O attract electrons by very different amounts (1.9 versus 3.44), so the bonding electrons are far from equally shared.

explanation: The difference is 3.44 − 1.9 = 1.54. That falls between 0.4 and 1.9, so the Si–O bond is definitely polar covalent.

prompt: Magnesium oxide, MgO, forms from magnesium (electronegativity 1.31) and oxygen (electronegativity 3.44). How would the bond between Mg and O be classified?

choices.text: Likely ionic
Definitely polar covalent
choices.why: Definitely polar covalent bonds have differences from 0.4 up to 1.9. The Mg–O difference, 3.44 − 1.31 = 2.13, is larger than that.

choices.text: Slightly polar covalent
choices.why: Slightly polar bonds have differences of 0.4 or less; 2.13 is far larger.

choices.text: Nonpolar covalent
choices.why: Mg and O attract electrons by very different amounts, so their electrons are not shared equally at all.

explanation: The difference is 3.44 − 1.31 = 2.13, which is greater than 1.9, so the bond is likely ionic: it is so polar that electrons actually transfer from Mg to O.

prompt: Bromine and chlorine combine to form bromine monochloride, BrCl. The electronegativity of Br is 2.96 and that of Cl is 3.16. How would the Br–Cl bond be classified?

choices.text: Slightly polar covalent
Nonpolar covalent
choices.why: Br and Cl attract electrons by slightly different amounts (2.96 versus 3.16), so the sharing is not perfectly equal.

choices.text: Definitely polar covalent
choices.why: Definitely polar bonds have differences above 0.4. The Br–Cl difference is only 3.16 − 2.96 = 0.20.

choices.text: Likely ionic
choices.why: Likely ionic bonds have differences greater than 1.9; 0.20 is tiny by comparison.

explanation: The difference is 3.16 − 2.96 = 0.20, which falls between 0 and 0.4, so the Br–Cl bond is slightly polar covalent, with Cl slightly δ−.

prompt: Which of these bonds is nonpolar covalent? Electronegativities: K 0.82, B 2.04, H 2.2, Cl 3.16.

choices.text: Cl–Cl
B–H
choices.why: The difference, 2.2 − 2.04 = 0.16, is small but not zero, so B and H do not share their electrons exactly equally.

choices.text: H–Cl
choices.why: The difference is 3.16 − 2.2 = 0.96, so the electrons are pulled noticeably toward Cl.

choices.text: K–Cl
choices.why: The difference is 3.16 − 0.82 = 2.34, greater than 1.9, so this bond is likely ionic.

explanation: A nonpolar covalent bond has an electronegativity difference of 0. The two Cl atoms in Cl–Cl are identical, so they attract the bonding pair equally and the difference is 3.16 − 3.16 = 0.

prompt: Which bond is the most polar? Electronegativities: Al 1.61, H 2.2, Br 2.96, N 3.04, Cl 3.16, O 3.44, F 3.98.

choices.text: Al–Cl
O–F
choices.why: F is the most electronegative element, but polarity depends on the difference: 3.98 − 3.44 = 0.54, much less than the Al–Cl difference of 1.55.

choices.text: H–Br
choices.why: The difference is 2.96 − 2.2 = 0.76, only about half the Al–Cl difference of 1.55.

choices.text: N–Cl
choices.why: N and Cl have nearly equal electronegativities; the difference is only 3.16 − 3.04 = 0.12.

explanation: The larger the electronegativity difference, the more polar the bond. The differences are Al–Cl 1.55, H–Br 0.76, O–F 0.54, and N–Cl 0.12, so Al–Cl is the most polar.

prompt: Silicon tetrachloride, SiCl4, contains four Si–Cl bonds. The electronegativity of Si is 1.9 and that of Cl is 3.16. What is the electronegativity difference for the Si–Cl bond?
explanation: Subtract the smaller electronegativity from the larger: 3.16 − 1.9 = 1.26. That puts the Si–Cl bond in the definitely polar covalent range, between 0.4 and 1.9.

prompt: A metal M forms a bond with fluorine, whose electronegativity is 3.98. Fluorine attracts the bonding electrons more strongly than M does, and the electronegativity difference for the bond is 3.19. What is the electronegativity of M?
explanation: Because F attracts the electrons more strongly, F has the higher electronegativity, so M = 3.98 − 3.19 = 0.79. With a difference greater than 1.9, this bond is likely ionic.

prompt: How can the polarity of covalent bonds affect a substance?

choices.text: If its molecules are polar overall, it may have higher melting and boiling points than expected.
If its molecules are polar overall, it will have lower melting and boiling points than expected.
choices.why: Polarity can raise a substance's melting and boiling points above what you might expect, not lower them.

choices.text: If its molecules are polar overall, it will dissolve in every other substance, including water and hexane.
choices.why: A polar substance may or may not be soluble in a given substance such as water or hexane; polarity doesn't make it dissolve in everything.

choices.text: Bond polarity has no effect on its properties; only the number of bonds in each molecule matters.
choices.why: The polarity of covalent bonds can have a significant influence on properties such as melting point, boiling point, and solubility.

explanation: The polarity of covalent bonds can strongly influence a substance's properties. If the overall molecule is polar, the substance may have a higher melting point and boiling point than expected, and polarity affects whether it dissolves in substances such as water or hexane.

prompt: What is the bond energy of a covalent bond?

choices.text: The approximate amount of energy needed to break the bond
The approximate amount of energy given off when the bond breaks
choices.why: Breaking a covalent bond takes energy rather than giving it off. Bond energy is the energy that must be supplied to break the bond.

choices.text: The difference in electronegativity between the two bonded atoms
choices.why: That difference measures how polar a bond is, not how much energy it takes to break.

choices.text: The energy needed to remove one electron from one of the bonded atoms
choices.why: Removing an electron from an atom is a different process. Bond energy is the energy needed to break the bond between two atoms.

explanation: Covalent bonds are stable, but they can be broken if enough energy is supplied. The approximate amount of energy needed to break a covalent bond is its bond energy, usually given in kJ/mol.

prompt: The O–H bond energy, 463 kJ/mol, is used to estimate energy changes involving O–H bonds in water, in methanol, and in many other molecules. Which statement about this value is correct?

choices.text: It is an average; the actual O–H bond energy varies slightly from one molecule to another.
It is the exact O–H bond energy in every molecule that has an O–H bond.
choices.why: Bond energies are average values. The exact energy of an O–H bond varies slightly among molecules, though it should be close to 463 kJ/mol.

choices.text: It applies only to water, so it can't be used for O–H bonds in other molecules.
choices.why: The approximate energy of a bond is similar whenever the same two atoms are bonded, so the value can be used for O–H bonds in many molecules.

choices.text: It is the energy needed to break all the bonds in one mole of water molecules.
choices.why: A water molecule, H–O–H, has two O–H bonds, so breaking all of its bonds takes about twice 463 kJ/mol. The value is for one mole of O–H bonds.

explanation: The exact energy of a bond depends slightly on the molecule, but it is similar whenever the same two atoms are bonded. Tabulated bond energies are therefore average values, which is why estimates made with them are only approximate.

prompt: For bonds between the same two elements, how do the bond energies of single, double, and triple bonds compare?

choices.text: The triple bond has the highest energy and the single bond the lowest, with the double bond in between.
The single bond has the highest energy and the triple bond the lowest, with the double bond in between.
choices.why: It is the other way around: sharing more pairs of electrons makes the bond harder to break. C–C is 348 kJ/mol, but C≡C is 837 kJ/mol.

choices.text: All three have about the same energy, because the same two elements are bonded in each case.
choices.why: The number of shared pairs matters. A double bond is stronger than a single bond, and a triple bond is stronger than a double bond.

choices.text: The double bond has exactly twice the single bond's energy, and the triple bond exactly three times.
choices.why: The order is right, but the energies of multiple bonds are not exact multiples of the single bond energy.

explanation: For bonds involving the same two elements, a double bond is stronger than a single bond, and a triple bond is stronger than a double bond. For carbon, C–C is 348 kJ/mol, C=C is 611 kJ/mol, and C≡C is 837 kJ/mol.

prompt: Bond energies: C–C 348 kJ/mol, C≡C 837 kJ/mol, N–N 163 kJ/mol, N≡N 946 kJ/mol. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: C≡C is less than three times as strong as C–C, but N≡N is more than three times as strong as N–N.
C≡C is more than three times as strong as C–C, but N≡N is less than three times as strong as N–N.
choices.why: This swaps the two: 3 × 348 = 1,044 kJ/mol, which is more than 837, while 3 × 163 = 489 kJ/mol, which is less than 946.

choices.text: C≡C is exactly three times as strong as C–C, and N≡N is exactly three times as strong as N–N.
choices.why: Multiple bond energies are not exact multiples: 3 × 348 = 1,044 is not 837, and 3 × 163 = 489 is not 946.

choices.text: C≡C is more than three times as strong as C–C, and N≡N is more than three times as strong as N–N.
choices.why: That is true for nitrogen (946 is more than 489) but not for carbon: 837 kJ/mol is less than 3 × 348 = 1,044 kJ/mol.

explanation: Three times C–C is 3 × 348 = 1,044 kJ/mol, more than the C≡C value of 837, while three times N–N is 3 × 163 = 489 kJ/mol, far less than the N≡N value of 946. Multiple bond energies are not exact multiples of the single bond energy.

prompt: Methanol has the structure H3C–O–H: a C atom bonded to three H atoms and joined by a single bond to an O atom, which carries one H atom. Bond energies: C–H 414 kJ/mol, C–O 351 kJ/mol, C=O 799 kJ/mol, O–H 463 kJ/mol. Which bond in methanol is the strongest?

choices.text: The O–H bond
The C=O bond
choices.why: C=O has the largest energy listed, but methanol has no C=O double bond; its C and O atoms are joined by a C–O single bond.

choices.text: A C–H bond
choices.why: At 414 kJ/mol, a C–H bond takes less energy to break than the O–H bond at 463 kJ/mol.

choices.text: The C–O bond
choices.why: At 351 kJ/mol, the C–O single bond is the weakest of methanol's bonds.

explanation: The strongest bond is the one that needs the most energy to break. Methanol's bonds are C–H (414 kJ/mol), C–O (351 kJ/mol), and O–H (463 kJ/mol), so the O–H bond is the strongest.

prompt: Which statement about the energy of breaking and making covalent bonds is correct?

choices.text: Breaking a bond is endothermic, with a positive ΔH; making a bond is exothermic, with a negative ΔH.
Breaking a bond is exothermic, with a negative ΔH; making a bond is endothermic, with a positive ΔH.
choices.why: This is reversed. Energy must be supplied to break a covalent bond, and energy is given off when one forms.

choices.text: Breaking and making a bond are both endothermic, since each one changes the molecule's structure.
choices.why: Only bond breaking requires energy. Making a covalent bond always gives off energy, so it is exothermic.

choices.text: Breaking a polar bond is exothermic, but breaking a nonpolar bond is endothermic, with a positive ΔH.
choices.why: Polarity doesn't change the sign: breaking any covalent bond requires energy, so it is always endothermic.

explanation: Covalent bonds always require energy to be broken, so bond breaking is endothermic and its ΔH is positive. When a covalent bond is made, energy is always given off, so bond making is exothermic and its ΔH is negative.

prompt: Silane, SiH4, has four Si–H single bonds, and the Si–H bond energy is 293 kJ/mol. Estimate ΔH for forming 1 mol of SiH4 from separate Si and H atoms, so that all four Si–H bonds are made. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Making covalent bonds is exothermic, so each mole of Si–H bonds formed has ΔH ≈ −293 kJ. One mole of SiH4 contains four moles of Si–H bonds: 4 × (−293 kJ) = −1,172 kJ.

prompt: For a certain reaction, an estimated 1,850 kJ is needed to break the bonds in the reactants, and an estimated 2,120 kJ is given off as the bonds in the products form. What is the estimated ΔH of the reaction?

choices.text: −270 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic
+270 kJ, so the reaction is endothermic
choices.why: Bond breaking counts as positive and bond making as negative: +1,850 kJ + (−2,120 kJ) = −270 kJ. More energy is given off than is absorbed.

choices.text: +3,970 kJ, so the reaction is endothermic
choices.why: The energy given off by forming bonds is a negative energy change, so it can't be added to the bond-breaking energy as a positive number.

choices.text: −3,970 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic
choices.why: Bond breaking is endothermic, so its 1,850 kJ counts as positive; only the bond-making energy is negative.

explanation: Combine the positive energy change for breaking bonds with the negative energy change for making bonds: +1,850 kJ + (−2,120 kJ) = −270 kJ. The negative ΔH means the reaction is exothermic.

prompt: Estimate ΔH for H2 + F2 → 2HF. The molecules are H–H, F–F, and H–F, and the bond energies are H–H 436 kJ/mol, F–F 159 kJ/mol, and H–F 569 kJ/mol. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Bonds broken: 1 H–H + 1 F–F = 436 + 159 = +595 kJ. Bonds formed: 2 H–F = 2(569) = 1,138 kJ given off, or −1,138 kJ. ΔH ≈ +595 + (−1,138) = −543 kJ.

prompt: Estimate ΔH for N2 + 2H2 → N2H4. N2 has a triple bond (N≡N), each H2 is H–H, and hydrazine, N2H4, has the structure H2N–NH2: an N–N single bond with two H atoms bonded to each N atom. Bond energies: N≡N 946 kJ/mol, H–H 436 kJ/mol, N–N 163 kJ/mol, N–H 389 kJ/mol. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Bonds broken: 1 N≡N + 2 H–H = 946 + 2(436) = +1,818 kJ. Bonds formed: 1 N–N + 4 N–H = 163 + 4(389) = 1,719 kJ given off, or −1,719 kJ. ΔH ≈ +1,818 + (−1,719) = +99 kJ, so the reaction is endothermic.

prompt: Estimate ΔH for the combustion of methane, CH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O. CH4 has four C–H bonds, each O2 is O=O, CO2 is O=C=O, and each H2O is H–O–H. Bond energies: C–H 414 kJ/mol, O=O 498 kJ/mol, C=O 799 kJ/mol, O–H 463 kJ/mol. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.

Hydrogen peroxide decomposes by 2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2. H2O2 has the structure H–O–O–H, H2O is H–O–H, and O2 is O=O. Bond energies: O–H 463 kJ/mol, O–O 146 kJ/mol, O=O 498 kJ/mol. Estimate ΔH for the reaction as written. Give ΔH in kJ, with a minus sign if it is negative.
explanation: Bonds broken: two H2O2 molecules have 4 O–H + 2 O–O = 4(463) + 2(146) = +2,144 kJ. Bonds formed: 4 O–H + 1 O=O = 4(463) + 498 = 2,350 kJ given off, or −2,350 kJ. ΔH ≈ +2,144 + (−2,350) = −206 kJ.

prompt: A student estimates ΔH for N2 + 3H2 → 2NH3, where N2 is N≡N, each H2 is H–H, and each NH3 has three N–H bonds. The student writes: bonds broken = 1 N≡N + 3 H–H = 946 + 3(436) = 2,254 kJ; bonds formed = 3 N–H = 3(389) = 1,167 kJ; ΔH ≈ 2,254 − 1,167 = +1,087 kJ. What is the student's mistake?

choices.text: Two NH3 molecules form, so six N–H bonds are made, not three.
The N≡N bond energy should be three times the N–N single bond energy.
choices.why: Multiple bond energies are not exact multiples of single bond energies. The N≡N value of 946 kJ/mol is the right one to use.

choices.text: The energy of the bonds formed should be added to the energy of the bonds broken.
choices.why: Bond making is exothermic, so its energy counts as negative. Subtracting it from the bond-breaking energy is correct.

choices.text: Only one H–H bond breaks, because all the H atoms end up together in NH3.
choices.why: Each of the three H2 molecules has one H–H bond, and all three must break so the H atoms can bond to N.

explanation: Each NH3 has three N–H bonds and the equation makes two NH3 molecules, so 6 N–H bonds form: 6(389) = 2,334 kJ. The estimate becomes ΔH ≈ 2,254 − 2,334 = −80 kJ, an exothermic reaction.

prompt: A student estimates ΔH for H2 + O2 → H2O2, where hydrogen peroxide has the structure H–O–O–H. Bond energies: H–H 436 kJ/mol, O–O 146 kJ/mol, O=O 498 kJ/mol, O–H 463 kJ/mol. The student writes: bonds broken = 1 H–H + 1 O–O = 436 + 146 = 582 kJ; bonds formed = 2 O–H + 1 O–O = 2(463) + 146 = 1,072 kJ; ΔH ≈ 582 − 1,072 = −490 kJ. What is the student's mistake?

choices.text: The bond broken in O2 is a double bond, so 498 kJ should be used, not 146 kJ.
The bond formed in H2O2 is an O=O double bond, so 498 kJ should be used for it.
choices.why: In H–O–O–H the two O atoms are joined by a single bond, so 146 kJ is correct for the O–O bond formed.

choices.text: The bonds formed should be counted as positive, since energy is needed to make bonds.
choices.why: Making covalent bonds gives off energy, so the bonds formed count as negative, just as the student had them.

choices.text: Only one O–H bond forms, since the H2 molecule had only one bond to begin with.
choices.why: When the H–H bond breaks, each H atom bonds to a different O atom, so H–O–O–H has two O–H bonds and 2(463) is correct.

explanation: O2 has a double bond, O=O, so breaking it takes 498 kJ. The corrected estimate is bonds broken = 436 + 498 = 934 kJ and bonds formed = 2(463) + 146 = 1,072 kJ, so ΔH ≈ 934 − 1,072 = −138 kJ.
